newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Army's top enlisted man hit with sex charges.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Army's top enlisted man hit with sex charges.

text.p: The Army said on Tuesday its top enlisted man will remain on duty at the Pentagon while it investigates "serious" sexual harassment charges leveled against him by a retired female soldier.

Army Sgt. Maj. Gene McKinney denied accosting a female sergeant major in a hotel in Hawaii last year and remained on the job as the top enlisted adviser to senior Army leadership. But he asked to be relieved of his duties on a panel reviewing sexual harassment policies in the service.

It was the latest allegation in a scandal that began in November 1996 when male trainers at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground training centre in Maryland were charged with harassing and even raping female recruits.

"We consider this set of allegations serious, just as any other set of allegations that have been received since November," Maj. Joe Piek, an Army spokesman at the Pentagon, said. "He (McKinney) is continuing his duties as sergeant major of the Army."

The Army said a 13-page document of allegations by Brenda Hoster, a 22-year veteran who retired last year after reaching the rank of sergeant major, had been turned over to the service's Criminal Investigative Division (CID).

Hoster was quoted as telling the New York Times in an interview published on Tuesday that McKinney grabbed and kissed her in a hotel room in Hawaii in April 1996 but left when she rejected his sexual advances. His wife was in a room just down the hall at the time, Hoster reportedly said.

Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters in response to questions that new Defence Secretary William Cohen was concerned over the allegations. But Bacon stressed "these are charges, they are not proven."
"Secretary Cohen is very concerned about these charges. He is very concerned about sexual harassment. He has made it clear that he has a zero tolerance policy," Bacon said.

Cohen expressed revulsion at intolerance, harassment or hazing last Friday after videotapes were shown on television of young Marines having parachute medals ground into their chests in bloody graduation rituals in 1991 and 1993.
Army officials said the service learned of the allegations involving McKinney on Monday and the CID quickly launched an investigation.

McKinney, whose Pentagon office is directly across from that of Army chief of staff Gen. Dennis Reimer, "denies he ever engaged in any form of sexual misconduct or improper treatment with the retired sergeant major who made the allegations," the Army said.

Hoster told the Times she decided to leave the service in August 1996 partly "for the good of the Army" and partly because she feared no one would believe her if she pressed her case. But she said she decided she could no longer remain silent when Army Secretary Togo West appointed McKinney, 46, to a senior panel gathered to investigate sexual harassment.
Bacon declined to comment on charges by Hoster that senior Army officials tried to circumvent an investigation of McKinney.
The Army, meanwhile, announced on Tuesday that a seventh male instructor was charged at Aberdeen last week in the sexual harassment scandal that erupted in November.
